title: History and Collective Memory
description: A university seminar on how societies remember the past, from memorials and oral history to the debate about statues.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Who owns the past?
parts.intro: You will hear a professor opening a seminar on collective memory.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: Welcome to the seminar. This term we're asking a deceptively simple question: who owns the past? Not who owns the archives, but who owns the stories a society tells itself about what happened.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: The concept of collective memory is usually traced to a French sociologist writing between the wars. His central claim was radical for its time: memory is not stored privately in individual heads, but shaped by the groups we belong to. We remember as members of families, villages, classes and nations.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: Consider how this works. You may believe you remember a family holiday vividly. But much of that vividness comes from the retelling, from the photographs on the wall, from the argument over whose version is right. The memory has been, quite literally, co-authored.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: Now scale that up. A nation also tells and retells. Anniversaries, textbooks, films, monuments, even the names of streets, all rehearse a particular account of the past, and, crucially, a particular account of who we are.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: I should distinguish this from history. History, at least in aspiration, is a discipline of evidence: it welcomes doubt and revises itself. Collective memory is a living practice, and it prefers clarity. It likes heroes, villains and turning points. Historians often find themselves unwelcome at commemorations for precisely this reason.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: I don't want to suggest, though, that memory is simply history's inferior cousin. Without it, the past would be inert, a heap of documents nobody feels responsible for. Memory is what makes the past matter. The trouble is that mattering and accuracy do not always travel together.

parts.title: Part 2 · Memorials and forgetting
parts.intro: You will hear a student, Minh, discussing memorials with Professor Whitfield.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Professor, can I push back on that distinction? Doesn't history itself get shaped by nations? Textbooks are written by governments, after all.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: A good objection, Minh. History as an institution is certainly not innocent. Governments fund archives, set curricula and decide what's taught to ten-year-olds. So I'd say the line is blurred in practice, though still worth drawing in principle.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Why worth drawing, if it's blurred?

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: Because it gives us a standard to appeal to. If a commemoration claims something that the evidence contradicts, historians can say so. Without a distinction, every account is just one more story, and the loudest wins.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: I was reading about a war memorial in a small town in the north. The names of the fallen were carved, but it said nothing about the soldiers who were executed for desertion.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: A classic case. Memorials tend to remember sacrifice and forget shame. Decades later, families campaigned for those men to be pardoned, and the debate was less about the soldiers than about what the nation wanted to believe about itself.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: So forgetting isn't accidental.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: Sometimes it's accidental, but often it's organised. Societies need to forget certain things in order to move on, and that's not always sinister. After civil conflicts, for example, a measure of silence can keep the peace. The difficulty is that silenced stories rarely disappear. They resurface in the next generation, often angrier.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Like a debt that gathers interest.

script.speaker: Professor Whitfield
script.text: Rather a good image. Do write that down, but attribute it to yourself.

parts.title: Part 3 · Oral history
parts.intro: You will hear a lecturer, Dr Lowe, talking about spoken testimony as a historical source.

script.speaker: Dr Lowe
script.text: Let me turn to a source that historians once treated with suspicion: the spoken testimony of ordinary people. Oral history grew out of a conviction that official records are written by the powerful, and that the rest of the population is mostly absent from the archive.

script.speaker: Dr Lowe
script.text: When researchers began recording elderly workers, migrants and veterans in the middle of the last century, they were told, politely at first and then less politely, that memory is unreliable. And they agreed. Memory is unreliable. It compresses, rearranges and embellishes.

script.speaker: Dr Lowe
script.text: But they made a subtle argument. A mistake in testimony can be a clue rather than a defect. In one well-known study, interviewees in an industrial town placed a famous strike three years later than the documents showed, and attached it to a different outcome than the real one. That looks like carelessness until you realise what they were doing. They were moving the event to where it made emotional sense, to the moment when the community, in their eyes, lost its confidence.

script.speaker: Dr Lowe
script.text: In other words, the error told the historian what the strike meant, not when it happened. The document gave the date, and the testimony gave the significance.

script.speaker: Dr Lowe
script.text: There's an ethical side, too. Listening to testimony is not a neutral act. The interviewer chooses the questions, and often the silences. Some survivors of conflict I have worked with spoke for the first time only because someone finally stayed long enough to hear the end of a sentence.

script.speaker: Dr Lowe
script.text: I would add a caution. Testimonies can harden. A story told many times at commemorations, to journalists and schools, becomes smooth, a kind of performance. The most revealing interviews are often the first ones, before the story has found its shape.

parts.title: Part 4 · Should statues come down?
parts.intro: You will hear two historians, Dr Harris and Dr Ngoc, debating the removal of statues.

script.speaker: Dr Harris
script.text: I'll say it plainly: removing a statue is erasing history. If we start taking down every monument to someone with views we now find objectionable, there'll be no past left on the streets.

script.speaker: Dr Ngoc
script.text: I'd gently challenge the premise, Daniel. A statue isn't history, it's an honour. It was put there, usually generations after the person's death, by people who wished to celebrate them. Taking it down doesn't delete the archive. It changes who we choose to celebrate.

script.speaker: Dr Harris
script.text: But monuments also teach us something about the era that built them. Remove the statue and you remove the evidence of what that era admired.

script.speaker: Dr Ngoc
script.text: That's a better argument, and I take it seriously. Which is why many historians favour relocating monuments to museums, where they can be explained. A statue in a square says, this person is admirable. A statue in a gallery, with a label, says, this is what people once thought.

script.speaker: Dr Harris
script.text: My worry is that museums become graveyards for things we're embarrassed about, and that each generation will feel entitled to rewrite the street map to suit itself.

script.speaker: Dr Ngoc
script.text: Each generation already does. The statue was itself a rewrite. The question is whether the process is democratic and transparent, or the work of a crowd at midnight or a committee in secret.

script.speaker: Dr Harris
script.text: That I can accept. Process matters more than the verdict.

script.speaker: Dr Ngoc
script.text: I'd say they both matter. But I think we're agreeing that the worst outcome is silence, putting things in storage and hoping nobody asks.

script.speaker: Dr Harris
script.text: Then we agree on the destination, if not the route.

questions.text: What is the main idea of the professor's opening talk?
options: Memory of the past is shaped by groups and differs from history
Archives should be controlled by the people who use them most often
Individuals remember events more accurately than nations do
History is more reliable than any form of memory could be
questions.explanation: She introduces collective memory as something shaped by groups, and then distinguishes it from history as a discipline of evidence.

evidence.quote: memory is not stored privately in individual heads, but shaped by the groups we belong to

questions.text: What was the French sociologist's central claim?
options: Families remember more accurately than villages
Nations decide what individuals forget
Memory is shaped by the groups we belong to
Memory is stored privately in each person
questions.explanation: She says his claim was that memory is not private but shaped by groups such as families, villages, classes and nations.

evidence.quote: shaped by the groups we belong to

questions.text: What does the example of the family holiday show?
options: Photographs are the most reliable evidence of the past
Family arguments tend to damage the memory of events
People usually remember their holidays wrongly
Vivid memories often come from retelling and sharing
questions.explanation: She says the vividness comes from retelling, photographs and arguments, so the memory is co-authored.

evidence.quote: The memory has been, quite literally, co-authored.

questions.text: How does the professor regard collective memory?
options: As unimportant to the way modern societies work
As more accurate than the work of historians
As valuable, although accuracy is not guaranteed
As an inferior and misleading copy of real history
questions.explanation: She rejects the idea that memory is history's inferior cousin, saying it makes the past matter, though mattering and accuracy do not always go together.

evidence.quote: Memory is what makes the past matter.

questions.text: Why does the professor say historians are often unwelcome at commemorations?
options: To argue that historians should keep out of politics
To suggest that historians dislike taking part in any public events
To explain why commemorations are so expensive to organise
To show that memory wants clarity whereas history welcomes doubt
questions.explanation: She uses this to illustrate that memory likes heroes, villains and turning points, while history welcomes doubt and revises itself.

evidence.quote: Historians often find themselves unwelcome at commemorations for precisely this reason.

questions.text: Why does Minh mention textbooks written by governments?
options: To argue that textbooks are far too long for schoolchildren
To complain about the education he received himself
To challenge the separation of history from national memory
To show that governments tend to forget the past
questions.explanation: He questions the professor's distinction by pointing out that history is also shaped by nations through textbooks.

evidence.quote: Doesn't history itself get shaped by nations?

questions.text: How does the professor respond to Minh's objection?
options: She agrees that the distinction should now be abandoned
She rejects the objection completely and moves on
She accepts that the line is blurred but defends it as useful
She says that government textbooks are always accurate
questions.explanation: She calls it a good objection, says the line is blurred in practice, but argues it still gives a standard to appeal to.

evidence.quote: the line is blurred in practice, though still worth drawing in principle

questions.text: What did the war memorial fail to mention?
options: The names of the fallen
The towns in the north
The families who campaigned for a pardon
Soldiers executed for desertion
questions.explanation: Minh says the names of the fallen were carved, but nothing was said about the soldiers executed for desertion.

evidence.quote: it said nothing about the soldiers who were executed for desertion

questions.text: What does the professor suggest about forgetting?
options: It permanently removes difficult stories from a society's past
It is always accidental, never planned by those in power
It is always harmful to the peace of a society after conflict
It is often organised and useful, but silenced stories may return
questions.explanation: She says forgetting is often organised, can keep the peace, but silenced stories usually resurface angrier in the next generation.

evidence.quote: silenced stories rarely disappear

questions.text: How does the professor react to Minh's comparison with a debt?
options: She finds it confusing and asks him to explain
She thinks it is inaccurate for historical debts
She approves of it with some humour
She says it has been used many times before
questions.explanation: She calls it a rather good image and jokes that he should attribute it to himself.

evidence.quote: Rather a good image.

questions.text: Why did oral historians begin recording ordinary people?
options: They wanted to prove that memory was perfectly reliable
They were paid by governments to collect testimony
They found that many written archives were destroyed
They believed official records were written by the powerful
questions.explanation: Dr Lowe says oral history grew from a conviction that official records are written by the powerful and ordinary people are mostly absent.

evidence.quote: official records are written by the powerful

questions.text: What does the study of the industrial strike show?
options: The strike was moved by the town's leaders to hide it
Errors in testimony can reveal what an event meant to people
Interviewees deliberately lied to the researchers involved
Documents are less reliable than memory in every case
questions.explanation: He says the error told the historian what the strike meant, not when it happened.

evidence.quote: the error told the historian what the strike meant, not when it happened

questions.text: What does Dr Lowe imply about interviewing?
options: It should only be done by professionally trained doctors
It is a neutral way of collecting plain facts
It works best when the interviewer stays silent throughout
The interviewer's choices influence what is said
questions.explanation: He says listening is not neutral, because the interviewer chooses the questions and often the silences.

evidence.quote: Listening to testimony is not a neutral act.

questions.text: Why does Dr Lowe mention survivors who spoke for the first time?
options: To show that patient listening can make testimony possible
To criticise earlier historians for lacking patience with survivors
To prove that survivors would rather stay silent
To argue that interviews must be kept short
questions.explanation: He says they spoke only because someone stayed long enough to hear the end of a sentence.

evidence.quote: someone finally stayed long enough to hear the end of a sentence

questions.text: Why are the first interviews often the most revealing?
options: The interviewers tend to ask much better questions
The story has not yet become a smooth performance
The witnesses are younger and remember more clearly
The documents are still fresh in the archive
questions.explanation: He explains that stories told repeatedly become smooth and performed, so early interviews are more revealing.

evidence.quote: before the story has found its shape

questions.text: What is Dr Harris's view at the start of the debate?
options: Statues are unimportant to historians
Statues should be moved to private collections
Modern leaders should choose which statues remain
Removing statues amounts to erasing history
questions.explanation: He says plainly that removing a statue is erasing history and that no past would be left on the streets.

evidence.quote: removing a statue is erasing history

questions.text: Why does Dr Ngoc say a statue is an honour, not history?
options: To suggest that statues are always built by governments
To prove that statues are inaccurate portraits of the dead
To claim that no statue should ever be built
To argue that removal does not delete the historical record
questions.explanation: She says a statue celebrates someone and removing it does not delete the archive, only changes who we celebrate.

evidence.quote: Taking it down doesn't delete the archive.

questions.text: What do many historians prefer to do with controversial monuments?
options: Replace them with larger statues of other people
Leave them in place without any explanation at all
Move them to museums where they can be explained
Store them out of sight until the debate ends
questions.explanation: Dr Ngoc says many historians favour relocating monuments to museums, where labels can explain them.

evidence.quote: many historians favour relocating monuments to museums

questions.text: What does Dr Ngoc mean by saying the statue was itself a rewrite?
options: Building monuments already reflects a later generation's choices
The statue was built in order to be removed later
The statue was copied from an earlier statue elsewhere
The statue was inaccurate in its appearance and style
questions.explanation: She means that putting up a statue was a decision by people long after the event, so changing monuments is nothing new.

evidence.quote: The statue was itself a rewrite.

questions.text: What do the two historians agree on at the end?
options: Museums should avoid displaying controversial objects
The worst outcome is silence, with problems hidden away
Statues should never be moved from public squares
Crowds should decide which monuments are removed
questions.explanation: Dr Ngoc says the worst outcome is silence and storage, and Dr Harris says they agree on the destination.

evidence.quote: the worst outcome is silence
